item.title: Prioritize CVE-2026-133311 as part of an exploited MiCollab cluster
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Prioritize CVE-2026-133311 as part of an exploited MiCollab cluster

A vulnerability management queue can make CVE-2026-133311 look easy to defer. Mitel rates the MiCollab AWV issue 5.9, describes a high-complexity attack and limits the direct impact to sensitive information disclosure. The CVE alone does not receive a critical score. The surrounding evidence changes the priority. The same advisory contains command-execution issues, the five-CVE set has been exploited, and CISA ADP marks exploitation as active.

That is not an argument for treating every medium issue as critical. It is an argument for grouping related findings when the vendor and attackers treat them as a set. A patch program that ranks each CVE in isolation may postpone the authentication flaw while a critical sibling is remediated. If both are fixed by the same advisory and affect the same component, splitting the work can leave a prepared or partially patched path behind.

What belongs in the risk record

Record the CVE's own facts first. CVE-2026-133311 is CWE-1390 weak authentication, affects MiCollab through 10.3 (10.3.0.18), requires a specific generated identifier or pre-staged content, and can disclose sensitive information. The CVSS 3.1 vector is network reachable, high complexity, no privileges and no user interaction, with high confidentiality impact only. Mitel's patch for 10.3.0.18 or a later supported release is the remediation path.

Then record the portfolio context. MISA-2026-0012 includes CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133324. The first, second, fourth and fifth cover upload, XML injection, command injection and authentication bypass. Mitel says exploiting them together can significantly amplify impact. CERT-In reports known exploitation. APEX Labs published an intrusion timeline and CISA KEV references.

The risk record should describe both levels. It should not claim that the medium CVE alone caused the critical outcome. It should explain why the same exposed component and patch cycle create a common remediation boundary.

Prioritization questions

Is the affected component reachable from the internet or from an untrusted partner network? Does the server integrate with Active Directory or store credentials for other systems? Is the version at or below 10.3.0.18? Has the vendor patch been verified rather than assumed from a build label? Are upstream logs available and retained long enough to investigate exploitation before the patch window?

If AWV is externally reachable and the version is unpatched, contain first and investigate immediately. If the component is not externally reachable, still apply the vendor fix and verify that no secondary path exists through a proxy or gateway. The CVSS score informs severity, but reachability, identity integration and known exploitation set the operational timeline.

Evidence that supports urgency

The CVE record's CISA ADP entry references the Accenture report and the KEV catalog, and its SSVC content marks exploitation as active. SecurityWeek reports that all five MiCollab flaws were added to KEV. APEX Labs observed a web shell before Mitel published the advisory and reported a second server communicating with the same actor infrastructure.

ZoomEye returned 730,707 matches for http.body="MiCollab" and zero matches for vul.cve="CVE-2026-133311". The page-body count indicates a broad searchable product presence, not a confirmed vulnerable population. It should not be used as a risk multiplier by itself. Internal inventory and version evidence are more defensible.

Remediation standard

Define completion as a supported patched build, verified on every production node, with all publication paths accounted for. Apply the 10.3.0.18 patch or move to a later release. Restrict external AWV access until validation is complete. Preserve evidence from systems that may have been compromised before the patch.

After remediation, review the LDAP connector and other reachable secrets. Examine proxy and identity logs for pre-patch activity. If the organization uses a KEV deadline, track the application patch and the incident investigation as separate workstreams. Closing the vulnerability ticket does not close a possible intrusion.

The priority statement should be concise: CVE-2026-133311 is a medium authentication flaw in an actively exploited multi-CVE MiCollab set. Remediate it with its sibling CVEs and treat exposed, unpatched servers as potential compromise cases.

References

- https://www.mitel.com/support/security-advisories/mitel-product-security-advisory-misa-2026-0012

- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CVEProject/cvelistV5/main/cves/2026/133xxx/CVE-2026-133311.json

- https://www.cert-in.org.in/s2cMainServlet?pageid=PUBVLNOTES01&VLCODE=CIVN-2026-0580

- https://accenture.github.io/cyber-intelligence/micollab-exploitation/

item.title: Why Zero-Login, Sub-100ms Web Tools Beat Heavy Apps for Mobile-First STEM Students
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Across South Asia and emerging education markets, the biggest barrier to quality university admission preparation is rarely a lack of motivation—it is friction.

Most commercial EdTech platforms follow a familiar playbook: require students to download a 120MB mobile app, create an account with phone verification, and hit a subscription paywall before they can check a single past-year question or eligibility rule. For a high-school student on a budget Android phone and an unstable 4G connection, that friction is often enough to make them give up.

While building Shikka.bd, an open-access university admission and 3D STEM learning hub, we tested the opposite approach: zero-login, sub-100ms web tools designed specifically for mobile-first students.

1. The Hidden Cost of "App-Only" Education

When a student searches Google at midnight for "DU admission negative marking rules" or "National University merit score calculation", they want an immediate, trustworthy answer—not an app store redirect.

Forcing an app install creates three problems:

- Storage & Data Overhead: Entry-level smartphones frequently run out of storage, causing students to uninstall heavy study apps between exams.

- Search Engine Invisibility: Content locked inside native apps cannot be indexed by search engines or screen readers, cutting off free organic discovery.

- Exclusion of Underserved Tracks: Commercial apps naturally prioritize high-margin engineering/medical coaching while neglecting massive student populations such as National University honours applicants.

2. Combining Static Speed with Interactive 3D STEM

Making a web platform fast does not mean stripping away interactivity. On Shikka.bd, we separated discoverable reference content from heavy simulation bundles:

- Instant Static Routes: Key guides—including the University Admission Eligibility Calculator, National University (NU) 200-Point Merit Hub, and past-year Question Bank—load directly from CDN edge HTML in under 100ms.

- Lazy-Loaded Interactive Visualizers: When a student opens a physics projectile simulation, a 3D biology model, or a geometric proof, the browser loads the Three.js and JSXGraph modules on demand without slowing down the initial page.

3. Designing for Trust and Accessibility

Students preparing for high-stakes exams need verified numbers, not guesses. Every formula, GPA threshold, and negative-marking rule should cite official university circulars clearly and work without requiring personal data or account sign-ups.

When EdTech teams remove login walls and optimize for sub-100ms web delivery, educational access expands immediately—especially for students who rely on shared devices or prepaid mobile data.

item.title: The Grim Reaper reviews my pull requests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

In an early PartySim build, adding a second drinks table took the simulated wait from three minutes to eight. The build passed.

Every year we throw a Halloween party for about 80 people. I built PartySim for it. Give it a floor plan and it builds a 3D haunted house full of simulated guests, so you can see where the party jams up.

I have a day job, so I set up Kiro Crew on my laptop to work through a queue while I was away. The jobs built changes, reviewed them and opened pull requests. I decided what got merged. Other people call this a software factory. For this project, we call it a haunted house.

the builds passed and the app was wrong

Early on I gave three models the same small feature. All three passed the build and linter. In the app, one worked, one was too faint to see, and one did nothing. Even the one that worked left this in its log:

Left undone: Visual verification at real size (server not started in this session)

The next night, three more features passed build and lint and still had problems I could see or hear in the app.

so the Grim Reaper looks at the app

For a visual change, the brief names one thing I should be able to see. A script opens the same URL and repeats the same clicks on the branch and on the commit where it split from main. The Grim Reaper reads the brief and the diff, then compares the screenshots. He writes PASS or FAIL with the screenshot and the file and line he checked. His agent is configured to write its findings in one folder:

{ "capability": "fs_write",

"match": ["docs/local/evidence/**"],

"effect": "allow" }

Back to the drinks table. Guests walking to a table didn't count toward its line, so too many picked the table that looked free. Pull request #6 counted guests on the way over and turned the table so its line ran onto the lawn. At the same minute of the same party, adding the second table now took the wait from three minutes down to two.

On another change, the brief asked for three lines of text to fit. They did. The extra line cut off the bottoms of the buttons below. The build and linter passed. The Reaper wrote FAIL.

who works in the haunted house

I handed Dracula a request or wrote the brief myself. Frankenstein, the Grim Reaper and the Ferryman ran on timers. They passed work through files and Git: a brief, a branch, screenshots and a review note. I handled the merge.

elsewhere in the house

The prompts and permissions live in .kiro/agents/. The roadmap is Markdown. For 102 of the 110 briefs in the build queue, we wrote out what to find and what to replace. That let me give Frankenstein the work on a small model at 0.06× Kiro credits.

what broke when I left it running

- When a Task Runner step failed, it ran a hard reset. That's why each build gets its own worktree.

- My first unattended jobs weren't allowed to read files. Each job needed its own tool allowlist.

- Jobs pause after two failures in a row. If I closed the laptop lid, the whole night shift stopped.

Between November 10 and 25, the Ferryman opened 103 pull requests. The PRs credit Frankenstein with 83 builds. Ninety-nine included screenshots, and 54 had a section for a screen that was supposed to stay the same.

I couldn't review them as fast as they came in. One evening I merged ten in the same second. I still have to work out how to give each one a proper look.

A screenshot also shows one moment. How do you test a queue that only starts backing up ten minutes into a simulation?

I used AI to help edit this post and illustrate the crew.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-28 19:37 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://dev.to/turbothomasnguyen/the-grim-reaper-reviews-my-pull-requests-hg

item.title: How you can spot and avoid scam ads on social media
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

How you can spot and avoid scam ads on social media

Convincing fake stores and AI-generated celebrity endorsements are making scam ads harder to recognize.

Imagine stumbling upon a Facebook ad for a jacket that's $300 under normal circumstances, going for a mere $39. With high-quality images and logos you recognize, plus a ticking clock to pressure you into buying within a short timeframe, these ads are often effective at getting you to act without thinking it through. But in most cases, that "bargain" is you handing over money to a fraudster.

Many people have fallen victim to scam ads on social media, some of which direct people to make a purchase from an external website. People reported losing over $95 million as a result of such purchases in 2025. Reported losses from all types of scams beginning on social media totaled $2.1 billion in the same year.

They may appear to be run by well-known and reputable businesses, sell nonexistent goods or feature fake celebrity endorsements (some created using AI). Many will direct you to a fake website, while others seek as many of your details as possible. As with most places online, having the word Sponsored simply means a fee has been paid to display the ad, so you need to investigate more to see whether it's legitimate.

Fake stores don't always look fake

Don't assume a phony site will be of poor quality and full of typos. Many scam ads will copy logos, images and their general look from the pages of well-known stores. Add large reductions with an offer counting down to "end of day", and they can be very convincing.

As recently as February 2026, Meta sued a Vietnam-based advertiser over a range of products purportedly available at reduced prices, including those of Longchamp. Shoppers completed a survey before reaching a site asking for credit card details. Meta said products were not delivered, but unauthorized recurring charges were made.

In separate cases, advertisers used manipulated images and voices of celebrities appearing to recommend healthcare products or lure victims into investment groups. With AI getting this good, classic giveaways like poor-quality images or awkward voiceovers aren't as common now.

The number of people affected by the Longchamp-style offers hasn't been disclosed. However, these are all good examples of how having the right logo and images, a well-produced clip with a celebrity or other recognizable features doesn't mean the source can be trusted.

Check the website, not just the discount

As a general rule, it's best to avoid clicking through to any website. Instead, type the name of the shop or store into a new tab and go directly to their homepage. This will help you avoid impersonator sites, though it's still possible to fall for a "discount" page that isn't claiming to be a well-known brand if you're not careful.

Look carefully at the URL, which may have additional or different words, spelling or domain ending to impersonate a genuine site. Try Googling the company name and "scam", "fraud" and similar words, and reading others' comments and experiences. Many fraudulent sites will use stock images or photos lifted from other companies, so it can also be worthwhile to do a reverse image search.

Don't assume that the presence of a padlock icon or "HTTPS" at the start of the URL means the company is reputable. HTTPS only encrypts your connection to the site, and scammers can use it too. A secure connection to a fraudulent site doesn't protect you from falling for it.

It's also useful to pause for a moment and apply some common sense. Always remember the old "too good to be true" line: luxury brands are not going to suddenly offer their goods at 80 percent off when the prestige is their main selling point.

If possible, you should always pay with a credit card (or wallet like PayPal) when buying from an unknown website, as that gives you more protection if you need to dispute any transactions. If you're asked to pay using unusual methods like gift cards or money transfers, you're almost certainly dealing with a scam. Gift card payments are a frequent tactic of scammers; legitimate companies won't ask you to pay with them.

Naturally, none of the above will be totally reliable indicators on their own every time. Still, it's well worth taking a short time to research a company before purchasing from them, rather than trying to get a refund or have a problem resolved for many weeks afterwards.

Clicked a scam ad? Here's what to do

In case you do open a shady website, don't enter your details or download any files. Double-check that nothing was downloaded, and decline any prompts to download programs. If something did get downloaded, don't open it. Delete it, then update and run an anti-malware scanner to make sure all is OK.

Entered a password or other details already? You should change those passwords, along with those for any other sites where you use the same password. If you've entered payment details, even if you didn't finish checking out, you should notify your bank or credit card company, explain what happened and ask them to prevent further payments. You can also ask them to reclaim any payments you made to the scam company.

Meta's page on fraudulent ads has links to report scam ads on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. TikTok's support also explains how to report an ad on that platform. Even after a report, you might see others like it, so keep your guard up.

It's also useful to take screenshots of the ad. Keep the URL of the website and details of any payments made, if they happened. You can report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Source: Engadget | Published: 2026-11-28 19:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.engadget.com/2326025/spot-and-avoid-social-media-scam-ads/

If you’ve been wondering which winged visitors have been frequenting your backyard, wonder no more as Birdbuddy’s entire lineup of smart feeders is discounted for Black Friday — including the recently released Nook and Home models. You have a few options to choose from, but our favorite, the Birdbuddy Nook, is on sale directly from Birdbuddy for $84.50 (about $85 off). The solar panel-equipped version is also down to $119 ($70 off), while the upgraded Birdbuddy Home — featuring a larger seed hopper, two solar panels, and support for 5GHz Wi-Fi — is going for $199 ($100 off).

Birdbuddy’s latest smart feeders are still at their low Black Friday prices

You can catch discounts on Birdbuddy’s entire line of bird feeders, with optional solar panels and 5GHz Wi-Fi upgrades.

Birdbuddy Nook

The Birdbuddy Nook is the company’s least expensive and smallest model, and it packs a lot of bang for your buck. Its 4K HDR camera delivers excellent image quality, and a 3.8-cup seed capacity means less frequent refills. An optional solar panel extends the already good battery life. Read our review.

Birdbuddy Home

The Birdbuddy Home has the same 4K HDR camera as the Nook, a larger 6.4-cup seed capacity, and support for both 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi.

If you’re curious about the differences between the available options, my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy compared both the Nook and Home to the older Pro Solar. She felt like the cameras weren’t as crisp on the newer models, and the viewing angle is narrower overall. The benefit to that compromise is that the cameras can now rotate 90 degrees, letting you capture birds as they fly and approach the feeder rather than only watching them chow down.

While both newer models are below the retail price of the older Pro Solar, that model is currently on sale on Amazon for $179.99 ($119 off), nearly matching its lowest price to date and making it an appealing option if you’re considering the Home. No matter which model you choose, you’ll need a paid membership to unlock all of Birdbuddy’s features, which include automatic photo and sound identification (free users can manually request identification), the ability to name birds yourself, and 2K ultra-resolution video. Individual plans start at $69.99 per year, while $98.99 per year grants family and friends access to livestreams and interaction; both the Nook and Home also include one free month of the Premium Family membership.

item.title: 5 Android Auto navigation apps you could be using instead of Google Maps
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, useful vocabulary

5 Android Auto navigation apps you could be using instead of Google Maps

Google Maps works just fine, but if you want something different that works with Android Auto, there are plenty of options.

Google Maps may be the one navigation app that comes with most Android phones, but that doesn't mean it has to be your default navigation app whenever you get in your car. Even with Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay, you might prefer another navigation app. Whether you have good reason to dislike Google Maps because of the way it works or you simply want something else to try, Android Auto supports alternatives like Waze, HERE WeGo, TomTom, MapQuest and Magic Earth. These apps look a bit different and offer distinct advantages, from privacy-focused features to offline maps and cleaner interfaces.

Sometimes, Google Maps won't do for driving in certain cities. It might work brilliantly for driving in New York City, for instance, but poorly in another part of the world. User numbers can also make a difference: more drivers using a crowdsourced navigation app can help improve its routing, as with Waze. Or maybe you're looking for a different app because you don't trust Google with your driving info. Or you might simply prefer how another app looks and works more than Google Maps. At the end of the day, that's exactly what matters most.

Waze

Waze built its reputation on community-powered traffic data and that continues to be its biggest draw. There are tons of reports from drivers about accidents, speed traps, police presence, road closures and real-time traffic jams. If you were avoiding Google Maps because you don't want all your data in Google's hands, then you're out of luck because Waze is owned by the tech giant. Still, there's no denying that there are some benefits to this, because the app uses Gemini-powered Conversational Reporting. This way, you can speak naturally about what you saw rather than take your eyes off the road to report an issue.

Waze also provides a cool feature called personalized navigation, which suggests routes based on your past trips, and a less chatty mode that trims down voice prompts while keeping essential turn alerts intact. Spend five minutes exploring the hidden features every Waze user should know about, and you will see you can change a ton of things, from how your car shows up on the map to the voice guiding you. Or maybe you want Christina Aguilera to tell you when to turn left, or you want to hear dad jokes while you drive. It's all in there.

You should know, however, that Waze doesn't really support offline navigation. An already-loaded route may keep working if you briefly lose data, but you can't download offline maps. You might also find the screen to be cluttered with alerts popping up constantly, which can be annoying if your car's infotainment screen is on the smaller side.

Here WeGo

Here WeGo takes a different approach to leading you places, leaning on frequently updated maps and decent global coverage rather than Waze-style community reports. It works with Android Auto for turn-by-turn navigation and features tons of business listings. You can also search for various other items nearby, like ATMs and pharmacies. Finding a gas station or a restaurant while you're driving somewhere will work well enough that you won't have to switch apps.

Offline maps are available for many countries; you can go completely offline on your travels once you've downloaded the maps, which is helpful if you're going to cross a border and perhaps face higher data costs. It's also ideal to use for areas with patchy mobile coverage. While Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you, Here WeGo has a simpler appeal. This isn't going to be the best app to use if you want to discover new places, but it will take you to your destination just fine — with fewer distractions.

TomTom

TomTom has been making GPS devices for decades, so naturally, its mobile app is a top contender as a Google Maps alternative for Android Auto. It's the same no-frills, distraction-free design, so you can focus on driving. If you find Google Maps too busy on your car's screen, TomTom's simpler interface might be enough reason to switch. You can also change your route if you need to and mark various issues like speed traps and closed roads. One of its better features is that when you choose a place you need to visit, the app lets you search for nearby parking. That's particularly handy when you're driving to a location you're unfamiliar with, so you don't have to go around the block a dozen times just to find available spots.

TomTom (formerly AmiGO) itself is free, but drivers who want more, like offline navigation, can pay for TomTom GO Expert. That one's built for truck drivers and other professionals, with features like routes tailored to a vehicle's height and weight, but you can definitely use it too if you really want.

MapQuest

MapQuest is another name that's been around since well before smartphones were a thing, and it's managed to stay relevant by adapting to modern driving habits. You can easily plan your route with the app, but it does come with the caveat that it's not a tool available worldwide. As long as you're driving in the United States or Canada, you're good to go. MapQuest gained Android Auto support in 2026, so you can finally take the app to the big(ger) screen in your car.…

item.title: Almost every great Black Friday deal is still happening this weekend
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, useful vocabulary

Black Friday has passed, but that doesn’t mean you missed out. Far from it. Almost all of the same deals from yesterday are still available, but some retailers plan to end theirs once the clock turns to early Sunday morning. True, expired deals you had your eye on are likely to return for Cyber Monday, though there’s no guarantee of that happening.

Almost every great Black Friday deal is still happening this weekend

Many of our favorite products are still cheaper than ever today, but several deals are flagged to end Sunday.

In the run-up to the event yesterday, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. For example, Apple’s latest MacBook Air recently fell to its pre-price-hike level for the first time since July. That’s a good deal to us, and several other discounts are still taking a similar shape, even as we approach Cyber Monday.

AirPods Pro 3

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

Anker Universal Charger (100W)

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader

With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering. It also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.

Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World Bundle

The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor

This curved 21:9 34-inch model uses the new (for 2026) Penta Tandem QD-OLED panel, which aims to deliver improved brightness and better handling of low light scenarios in games than the other QD-OLED monitors in this list.

HBO Max

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

Eufy Omni C28

The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.

SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

MSI Claw A8 gaming handheld

The AMD version of MSI’s late-2025 Claw handheld features the Ryzen Z2 Extreme, 24GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, plus an 8-inch 120Hz 1200p screen. It’s likely one of the best-performing handhelds at this price point.

Apple AirTag (second-gen)

Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera

The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage. Read our hands-on.

Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

Octobuddy Classic

Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.

Peacock

Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo.
